articles.text: The people of Charleston, S. C., are sorely afflicted. Four separate times last week they endured violent shocks of earth-quake, and now over 60,000 people there are living in tents or almost any cover, in the parks and streets. About one hundred persons have been killed and wounded by the shocks and a reign of terror is in progress.
articles.summary: Editorial note on the Charleston, S.C., earthquake: 60,000 people living in tents and about one hundred killed and wounded.

articles.text: The Democrats of Billings county will effect an organization on the 18th., to send delegates to the Aberdeen convention. Party politics will however, have little or nothing to do with county offices and we doubt if the time will ever come in Billings county when a party ticket is run and elected.
articles.summary: Billings county Democrats will organize on the 18th to send delegates to the Aberdeen convention; Packard doubts party tickets will ever matter in county offices.

articles.text: The citizens of the county should bestir themselves and hold a convention to elect delegates to the convention which is to nominate members of the Legislature. It is very likely that Billings county's two votes may have some weight in the convention and at any rate must "represent" if we wish to have any weight with the coming Legislature. As the only legislation we will need if any, will be in relation to the stock interest, we suggest that two of our stockmen would make good delegates and can think of no better names for the position than those of Howard Eaton and J. L. Truscott.
articles.summary: Packard urges a county convention to choose delegates to the legislative nominating convention and proposes stockmen Howard Eaton and J. L. Truscott.

articles.text: Ever since 1878, there have been cases pending, relative to the title to the land in Deadwood. The cases grew out of the filing of mineral claims on land in the business part of the city. The Hawkes claim especially, involving the best of the business part of Deadwood, has been bitterly contested. Numerous decisions have been rendered declaring that the land was mineral and now comes a final decision from Secretary Lamar to the same effect. Of course the title to the land takes the buildings along with it, and the business men will lose all the improvements they have put on the property.
articles.summary: Secretary Lamar issues a final decision declaring the Hawkes claim land in Deadwood's business district mineral land, costing business men their improvements.

articles.text: On Tuesday of this week, Frank Mead, well-known in the West-Missouri country and in 1884, Mayor of Mandan, shot and it is feared, fatally injured Frank Farnsworth, a dry-goods merchant of Mandan. The shooting took place in the lobby of the Merchant's hotel in St. Paul and was probably the result of a grudge borne by Mead, though Farnsworth says he does not know what it is. Mead is in jail and declares that the shooting was accidental as he only drew his revolver in sport. He had just before refused to shake hands with Farnsworth, however, and called him several vile names, so that it looks like a cold-blooded attempt at murder.
articles.summary: Former Mandan mayor Frank Mead shot Mandan merchant Frank Farnsworth in the Merchant's hotel, St. Paul, on Tuesday.

articles.text: There has been much talk among Stark county citizens, relative to having Villard county incorporated in their limits. The sentiment in Stark county relative to the stock interests, has repeatedly been shown to be of the kindliest nature, but we doubt if any advantage would be gained by Billings county from such an annexation. If any change is made, the limits of Billings county should be extended so as to include at least all of the Bad Lands and exclusively stock country. At present, our eastern line runs just to the west of Sully Springs, leaving a ragged edge of from three to ten miles of Bad Lands in Villard county. The citizens of Villard have also expressed a decided preference to being incorporated into Billings county, if any change is made. As they are the ones most vitally interested, their wishes should certainly be respected.
articles.summary: Packard argues that if Villard county is annexed, it should go to Billings county rather than Stark, so the whole Bad Lands lie in one stock county.

articles.headline: Communication.
articles.text:
Bismarck, Dak., Sep. 7, 1886.

A. T. PACKARD,
Editor Cow Boy:—
Your issue of the 20th. ult. contains the following article:

"The cases growing out of the citizens of Billings county refusing to pay taxes to Stark county, came up last week in Mandan. In the case of the N. P. Ref. Car Co., the preliminary injunction was sustained by Judge Francis and all the cases will come up at the next term of court."

In justice to ourselves, kindly make this correction. The suits of the Ref. Car Co., have been tried and are in the hands of the court for decision. We cannot afford to have the Company put in the eye of the public in the position the other suits occupy. The Ref. Car Co. has made no deposit of the amount claimed to be due from it for taxes and proposes to have a decision on their merits with its good piasters in its own coffers.

F. B. & E. S. ALLEN,
Atty's. N. P. Ref. Car Co.

The article quoted above, was based on one in the Mandan Pioneer, briefly stating the points involved in our article. Inquiry at the general office of the Company here showed nothing to the contrary and it was supposed that all the cases would come up for trial at the next term of court. From our correspondents it seems that a decision will soon be rendered by Judge Francis. This will be a definite pointer as to how the other cases will be decided, as the facts involved are exactly the same. The decision will be eagerly awaited by our citizens.
articles.summary: Attorneys for the N. P. Refrigerator Car Co. correct the Cow Boy: the company's Stark county tax suit has been tried and awaits Judge Francis's decision; Packard replies that the ruling will guide the other Billings county tax cases.

articles.text: The cattle market remains practically unchanged from last week and the advisability of shipping now is as doubtful as ever. In another column is found an article, under the head of "Beef Gathering," which is a fair presentment of both sides of the case from two conservative papers. "You pays your money and you takes your choice."
articles.summary: The cattle market is unchanged and the wisdom of shipping now remains doubtful.

articles.text: Fowler Bros., who now have a large pork-packing establishment in Chicago, are making preparations to open up one with a capacity of 3,000 hogs a day in St. Paul. At the same time, capitalists are said to be ready to put in slaughter-houses for cattle. This however, is only in the form of a rumor and the completion of a plant in St. Paul, competent to utilize the out-put of cattle from the northwest, seems as far off as ever. Especially to small outfits, such an establishment would be a god-send; saving many dollars on small shipments that must now go to Chicago. The same old difficulty of finding a profitable market, however, stares the promoters of such an enterprise in the face and makes of it a risky speculation. The only way in which we can see that the cattle traffic can be turned from its present channels, is by the adoption of a plan similar to the one now used by the N. P. Ref. Car Co., viz: to establish retail shops in the large cities, to be supplied from western abattoirs. There are now three of their shops running profitably in New York and there is no reason why others should not pay. If this plan is successful in the case of three shops, why should it not be in the case of 300, judiciously placed in eastern cities. As there is no lack of money back of the N. P. Ref. Car Co., we would not be surprised to see it take a leading part in such a move, with headquarters in Medora. At any rate, there seems no further room for new slaughter-houses, unless they do their own retailing.
articles.summary: On rumors of St. Paul packing houses, Packard argues the N. P. Refrigerator Car Co.'s model of retail shops in eastern cities (three now running in New York) is the way forward, perhaps headquartered at Medora.

articles.headline: The Time to Buy.
articles.text:
A man who had amassed a large fortune was asked by a young man to reveal the secret of money getting. "I will give it to you in a nutshell," said Money bags. "Buy when everybody wants to sell and sell when everybody wants to buy."

The "secret" thus disclosed suggests some singular truths. Whenever any particular industry is wonderfully prosperous capital rushes pell mell to get into it, and, although, as a rule, wealth is accumulated by industry and business prudence, those who have, by the exercise of those qualities achieved success, risk their slowly accumulated earnings with astonishing recklessness in schemes which promise unusual returns. The history of the range cattle business illustrates the pig-headed obstinacy of capital on the one hand and its mad recklessness on the other. For twenty years prior to 1880 the range cattle business was carried on with unvarying success. All the men engaged in it began poor and grew rich. Such uniform success and large profits were never before realized in the business. The industry was conducted openly, and its success and profits were generally known, and yet capital was indifferent to the advantages presented, and the stockmen were compelled to pay, and did pay, rates of interest that would have wrecked any other industry. But about the year 1880 the security and great profits of the business stood out so prominently that capital went crazy, and the men who would only risk their money in the business at exorbitant rates of interest with iron-clad security became anxious to become investors, and that, too, without ordinary business inquiry into details. The anxiety to become "cattle kings" became epidemic and the result inevitable. Ranges were crowded beyond their capacity, extravagant and fictitious prices were paid for both ranches and cattle. Many experienced cattlemen caught the infection, and waded beyond their [depth?]. A rigorous winter [depleted?] the herds. The profits realized when the business was conducted on a conservative and common-sense basis disappeared, and disappointment followed. There is nothing in all this which indicates that the range cattle business has changed in any of its essential features, nothing that indicates that it will not, under prudent management, be as safe and profitable as at any time in its history. But it does prove that there must be a return to common-sense methods. That many of those who engaged in the business when everybody was willing to sell are now willing to go out is doubtless true, and, therefore, the time to buy is at hand, and those who secure ranges and stock them within the safety line will realize old-time safety and profit.

It is natural to suppose that capitalists would take this view of it, but it is a historical fact that they don't. They go in when the hurrah is on, get out when disappointment comes and wait for the next excitement, and the men who hang to the willows and control their appetites for gain will go along making money.—[Colorado L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Colorado Live Stock Record arguing that after the post-1880 cattle boom and bust, now is the time to buy ranges and stock them prudently.

articles.headline: Beef-Gathering.
articles.text:
It seems that rangemen, particularly those along the line of the Union Pacific road, are inclined to be discouraged, and are thinking of opening the flood-gates and letting their cattle come to market regardless of condition or prices. At least this is the gist of the conclusions reached by very prominent managers. The reason given is that late rains on the prematurely cured grass has done more harm than good, having washed out much of the essential substance. In view of this fact and the present low prices, a number of cattlemen are said to have decided that there must be a rush of immature beeves to market, and that they had as well gather freely and take low prices early now as later in the season.

In this connection is the following from the Rocky Mountain Husbandman:

The question that presents itself is, shall they gather everything that is marketable or only the prime beef? We unhesitatingly say gather everything that will possibly do for the block. Gather the steers closely, including 3-year-olds and stags, also all the old dry cows. The loss in the winter and spring is largely of the offspring of dry cows, for they calve in early spring or late winter and are almost sure to lose their calves. If the weather is severe and feed scarce they will die also. Beef is low, very low, and prices are tending downward, while the market continues to grow weaker every day. But, for all that, it will be better to sell even at a low figure than endanger the whole herd by having the range overstocked.

The good advice above is not unmixed with evil. It is better to make bad beef of weaklings that could not stand the rigors of winter than to let them die on the range; and every precaution should be taken to prevent overstocking the ranges. But the object of stock raising is to put on the markets products that will bring to the producers the largest possible returns. This cannot be done by indiscriminately crowding forward the very kinds that are in least demand and the kinds which, if forced upon the trade, will injure the market for all below the very finest grades of stock. There are two classes into which range stock may be divided at market. Beef cattle, fat, or at least fleshy, and canning stock. Feeding cattle come in as a sub-class, as they sell inside of the range of prices for canners. Between the best canning cattle and the best range beef cattle there is usually a difference of about $1.00 to $1.25 per cwt. As a general thing, the best Wyoming range steers and good range cows will come in these two respective classes very nicely. But take a shipment of thin and medium steers, and they cannot class as beef cattle and are above the canning grade; thus coming between two classes of buyers and striking neither. Then all depends on the supply. Should such a lot happen here on a very light run and an advancing market, they would be taken by the men and forced to fill the places at good prices. But such conditions, as shippers well known, are only too rare, and [nine?] cases out of ten such cattle have to be sacrificed at about canning prices. The Journal urgently advises rangemen to carefully study and comply with the demands of the trade to avoid forcing "betwix and between" grades of cattle upon an over stocked market. If the rangers need relief, castrate the old bulls, spay the heifers, and place them on feed to fatten, but don't deliberately break down the beef market in taking care of the range, because the latter would be nothing without the former.—Montana L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Reprinted debate (Rocky Mountain Husbandman and Montana Live Stock Journal) on whether discouraged rangemen should ship everything or only prime beef this fall.

articles.text: The Marquise de Mores returned from New York last Thursday night. On Friday evening, the Duc and Duchesse de Luynes and their daughter and Count Suzannet stopped off and visited the Marquise over Sunday. M. de Saulty, who has been here for some time expecting to take a hunting trip to the Rocky mountains, accompanied them on their western trip, Monday evening.
articles.summary: The Marquise de Morès returned from New York; the Duc and Duchesse de Luynes, their daughter and Count Suzannet visited her over Sunday, then left west Monday with M. de Saulty.

articles.text: T. W. Gordon came in Tuesday from the west, having been to Helena and Butte. From his report, Butte seems to have recovered from its boom and there is plenty of work at good pay. He also says that judging from the looks of the range from the railroad, the grazing is constantly poorer as one goes west from Glendive. Several outfits are going to move their cattle south for winter feed.
articles.summary: T. W. Gordon returned Tuesday from Helena and Butte, reporting poor grazing west of Glendive and outfits moving cattle south for winter.

articles.text: The report comes in from the 13 camp that no horses are missing from there and that as a consequence Bob. Thompson could not have stolen any of them. The charge of horse-stealing is altogether too serious a one in this country to be lightly made and although we heard the matter definitely stated twice we concluded not to publish it. Just before going to press last week, however, we learned from a perfectly reliable source that the report was direct from the 13 camp. Even after the contradiction came in, we were assured that the charge was a true one, but the denial from the 13 camp settles it.
articles.summary: The 13 camp reports no horses missing, clearing Bob Thompson of a horse-stealing charge the paper had printed the previous week.

articles.text: While L. C. and Robert Hunt were loading a bunch of KC cattle at Dickinson, Tuesday, they received word from their sister Bessie at Fort Union, New Mexico, that their father had died there on that day. This death, following so close on that of their mother last winter, is a cruel blow and one which will attract the sympathy of all to the Hunt brothers. Both of them started immediately for New Mexico and will arrive there Saturday. Their father was Colonel in the regular army, stationed at Fort Vancouver, but for the last six months absent on sick leave. Their plans for the future are a little unsettled, but they will probably take their sister to Washington and then return here.
articles.summary: While loading KC cattle at Dickinson Tuesday, L. C. and Robert Hunt learned their father, an army colonel, had died at Fort Union, New Mexico; both left for New Mexico.
